title: Strings, bytes and runes — UTF-8 all the way down
summary: A Go string is a read-only byte slice holding UTF-8. len counts bytes, range walks runes, and case conversion is locale-blind — which matters if your users write Turkish.

examples.title: len counts bytes; range counts runes

annotations.note: len(s) is the byte length: 4 for "DİL", because İ encodes as two bytes. utf8.RuneCountInString counts the 3 characters.
range decodes UTF-8 and yields each rune with the byte offset where it starts: 0, 1, 3. The offsets skip 2, the second byte of İ.
Indexing returns a single byte (0xC4, half of İ). Decode from that offset to get the whole character back.

examples.title: Case conversion ignores locale until you ask for Turkish

annotations.note: strings.ToLower maps I to i whatever the user's language. The stdlib has the Turkish and Azeri mapping as unicode.TurkishCase: I becomes ı and İ becomes i (strings.ToUpperSpecial goes the other way).
Naive lowercasing turns both DIL and DİL into "dil", so a search for one finds the other. strings.EqualFold has no Turkish mode either: EqualFold("DİL", "dil") is false.

use_cases: Processing user input that is not pure ASCII: names, cities, addresses
Deciding between byte offsets (wire formats, file slices) and rune counts (UI limits)
Understanding why len('İ') == 2 and range treats it as one rune
strengths: One encoding everywhere: source and string literals are UTF-8 and the standard library assumes it; no separate wide-char type
range over a string just works for iteration; no manual decoder loops
Explicit byte/rune split makes costs visible instead of hidden in a locale setting
weaknesses: len and slicing are byte-based; s[:1] can cut a rune in half and produce invalid UTF-8
Locale rules are opt-in: Turkish needs strings.ToLowerSpecial(unicode.TurkishCase, s), other languages golang.org/x/text/cases, and EqualFold has no Turkish mode
Rune is an alias for int32, not a distinct type — the name suggests more safety than it delivers

pitfalls.title: Indexing a string gives a byte, not a character
pitfalls.detail: s[1] on "DİL" returns the first byte of İ (0xC4), which prints as garbage. Use []rune(s) or utf8.DecodeRuneInString when you need a whole character.

pitfalls.title: Counting characters with len
pitfalls.detail: len(s) is bytes. For UI length limits use utf8.RuneCountInString(s) — 'DİL' is len 4 but 3 runes.

quiz.why: İ encodes as two UTF-8 bytes, so the byte length is 4 even though there are 3 runes.

quiz.q: What does range yield for each iteration over a string?
quiz.why: range decodes UTF-8 and yields the starting byte index of each rune plus the rune itself — which is why indices skip over continuation bytes.

quiz.q: On a machine with a Turkish OS locale, what does strings.ToLower("ISTANBUL") return?
quiz.why: ToLower never consults the OS locale, so you always get 'istanbul'. Turkish rules need strings.ToLowerSpecial(unicode.TurkishCase, s).

further_reading.title: Go blog: Strings, bytes, runes and characters in Go

body:
## Concept

A Go string is a read-only slice of bytes, and those bytes are UTF-8. That
single decision explains most of this lesson: `len` counts bytes, indexing
gives bytes, and the `range` clause is the one construct that decodes runes
for you. A rune is a Unicode code point — `int32` under the alias — and the
conversion cost between "what the user sees" (runes) and "what the machine
stores" (bytes) is always visible in Go.

The second half is about case: Go's `strings` functions do simple, locale-blind
mapping. That is predictable and fast, but wrong for Turkish, where uppercase
`I` lowercases to dotless `ı` and dotted `İ` lowercases to plain `i`. The
standard library has that mapping as `unicode.TurkishCase`, used through
`strings.ToLowerSpecial` and `strings.ToUpperSpecial`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

C gives you `char*` and no encoding opinion — you already know the pain Go
avoids. Java and C# hide UTF-16 behind a `char` type, so you get a *different*
surprise (surrogate pairs) instead. Python 3 and JavaScript strings are
code-point-ish abstractions where indexing usually does what you mean; Go is
closer to the metal: bytes in memory, explicit decode on demand. If you have
fought `wchar_t` or ICU locale structs, Go's "one encoding, no guesses" stance
is a relief: Turkish casing is one stdlib call, and `golang.org/x/text` covers
other languages' rules when you need them.

## Design notes

The stdlib refuses to guess locales, so `strings.ToLower` never consults the
OS locale — the same binary behaves identically in Istanbul and Oslo. The
trade-off: correctness for Turkish users is *your* job, via
`strings.ToLowerSpecial(unicode.TurkishCase, s)` wherever text is normalized
for comparison or search. This matches Go's general philosophy of explicit
dependencies over ambient environment.

expected.len-range:
len: 4 runes: 3
byte 0: rune D
byte 1: rune İ
byte 3: rune L
t[1] as byte: 'Ä'
t[1] decoded: İ
expected.turkish-case:
ISTANBUL naive="istanbul" turkish="ıstanbul"
DIL naive="dil" turkish="dıl"
DİL naive="dil" turkish="dil"
naive merge:   true
turkish split: false
